metadata.title: Signals across the membrane (made up)
metadata.description: A made-up lecture with explanations, for the app's checks.

sections.title: Cyclic AMP as a second messenger

items.definition: A small molecule made inside the cell in response to a signal outside it, carrying that signal onward.
items.source_excerpt: A second messenger is a small molecule made inside the cell when a hormone binds outside; it carries the signal on.

items.definition: A second messenger made from ATP by adenylyl cyclase, which activates protein kinase A.
items.source_excerpt: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A.

items.definition: The enzyme that breaks cyclic AMP down to AMP, ending its signal.
items.source_excerpt: Phosphodiesterase breaks cyclic AMP down to AMP, which ends the signal.

items.title: Why the signal stops
items.text: Cyclic AMP is made only while the hormone keeps adenylyl cyclase switched on, and phosphodiesterase breaks it down all the time. So the signal lasts only as long as making outpaces breaking: block phosphodiesterase and cyclic AMP builds up, and the signal outlasts the hormone.
items.source_excerpt: Phosphodiesterase breaks cyclic AMP down to AMP, which ends the signal; caffeine blocks it.

items.question: A drug blocks phosphodiesterase. What happens to the cyclic AMP signal after the hormone is removed?
options: It outlasts the hormone, because cyclic AMP is no longer broken down
It stops at once, because adenylyl cyclase is switched off
It never starts, because cyclic AMP cannot be made
It is unchanged, because phosphodiesterase only acts on ATP
distractor_rationale: Switching off the maker does not remove what is already there
The maker is untouched; only the breaker is blocked
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cyclic AMP, not ATP
items.explanation: Cyclic AMP stays until something breaks it down.
items.source_excerpt: Phosphodiesterase breaks cyclic AMP down to AMP, which ends the signal; caffeine blocks it.

items.question: Which enzyme makes cyclic AMP from ATP?
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Phosphodiesterase
Protein kinase A
Calmodulin
distractor_rationale: It is what cyclic AMP activates
items.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP.
items.source_excerpt: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A.

items.question: Which of these are true of cyclic AMP?
options: Adenylyl cyclase makes it from ATP
It switches on protein kinase A
Adenylyl cyclase breaks it down once the hormone leaves
It acts by binding calmodulin
option_rationale: Adenylyl cyclase is the enzyme that converts ATP to cyclic AMP
Protein kinase A is what cyclic AMP activates
Adenylyl cyclase makes it; phosphodiesterase is what breaks it down
Calmodulin is calcium's partner, not cyclic AMP's
items.explanation: Cyclic AMP is made by adenylyl cyclase, acts through protein kinase A, and is ended by phosphodiesterase.
items.source_excerpt: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A.

items.definition: A second messenger that opens channels in internal stores, releasing calcium into the cytoplasm.
items.source_excerpt: Inositol trisphosphate opens channels in the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium.

items.definition: A protein that binds calcium and, once bound, switches on enzymes such as kinases.
items.source_excerpt: Calcium binds calmodulin, which then switches on kinases.

items.title: Calcium needs a partner
items.text: Calcium released from internal stores does little on its own: it acts by binding calmodulin, and calmodulin with calcium bound is what switches on the kinases. Unlike cyclic AMP, the messenger here is an ion, so the cell ends the signal by pumping it back into the stores rather than breaking it down.
items.source_excerpt: Calcium released from stores binds calmodulin, which then switches on kinases; pumps return calcium to the stores.

items.question: Calcium is released from internal stores, but calmodulin is missing. What happens to the kinases calmodulin switches on?
options: They stay off, because calcium acts through calmodulin
They switch on, because calcium binds kinases directly
They switch on, because inositol trisphosphate activates them
They stay off, because calcium is broken down at once
distractor_rationale: Calcium acts through calmodulin, not on kinases directly
Inositol trisphosphate only opens the calcium channels
Calcium is an ion: it is pumped back, not broken down
items.explanation: Without calmodulin, calcium has nothing to act through.
items.source_excerpt: Calcium released from stores binds calmodulin, which then switches on kinases; pumps return calcium to the stores.

items.question: A hormone makes a cell release calcium from its internal stores. Which of these are true of that calcium signal?
options: Inositol trisphosphate opened the channels that let the calcium out
The calcium switches on kinases by first binding calmodulin
The signal ends when pumps return the calcium to the stores
The signal ends when phosphodiesterase breaks the calcium down
The calcium switches on kinases directly, with no partner
option_rationale: Inositol trisphosphate opens the channels in the endoplasmic reticulum
Calcium acts through calmodulin, which then switches on the kinases
Calcium is an ion, so the cell pumps it back into the stores
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cyclic AMP; an ion cannot be broken down
Calcium needs calmodulin: on its own it does little
items.explanation: Inositol trisphosphate lets calcium out, calmodulin carries its signal to the kinases, and pumps end it.
items.source_excerpt: Calcium released from stores binds calmodulin, which then switches on kinases; pumps return calcium to the stores.
